Discuss the relational engine data model and access boundaries before resuming the predicate inventory review. Keep the architecture undecided until discussed. Append subsequent user and assistant discussion verbatim, with speaker labels; do not replace earlier entries with summaries.

## Discussion — 29 October 2026

### User

> **I would call the Activity board control “Filter.”** Filtering can apply to the complete accessible dataset, including data not yet fetched. Fetching determines how we obtain the matches; filtering describes what the user is doing.

Filter it is then.

> **Graph has no `item` because that row describes constructing the whole graph:** choosing sources, traversing relations, and returning nodes and edges. It runs once for the result. A graph’s individual node or edge filter would instead follow `(item, scope) => boolean`. Those are different operations, and the inventory should make that distinction clearer.

is it how we want to present things to the user though. In the end i consider it like a filter the same way activity board filter can fetch more data it already as, it would make sense for graph to be able to do the same and work like activity board filter. What it does is trigger the visibility of node in the graph.

Overall the inventory shows a non uniformity of how we layer view over relational engine and thats not surprising considering the history of the project and how we made it evolve and how blurry things still are on that front.

There is clearly a fundamental question overall. Should everything be entity / node / component / ... And everything we build is layered on top. Or do we allow any bypass of the graph layer. The materialization aspect is aswell i think quite the challenge honestly. It seems soo wastefull to have things that exist outside the graph and duplicating it inside the graph and synchronizing it in some case. Finally what check do we need to enforce our architecture choice ? I think until we answer those question and their impact foundation will stay brittle.

Lets do a task to discuss exactly just that as a child of graph://planning-26535745-4644-4770-af7c-1980c773377b/entries/af974474-bcbc-4144-b4a2-2300a9e8add8.json

because i can't really review the predicate until we discuss that.

I would call it "Refine relational engine data model".  Create the task and write down the discussion we have verbatim going forward in the task description.

### Assistant

The graph can use the same Filter presentation as the Activity board: the predicate determines visibility, and obtaining the data needed to evaluate it is a separate responsibility. My previous signature exposed an implementation distinction too early.

I suggest we start with one distinction: must all view access go through the relational engine, and must all underlying data be stored in it? Those are separate choices. We can then decide which projections or caches are justified, who owns their freshness and mutations, and which checks enforce those boundaries. The predicate signatures should follow those decisions.

### User

> I suggest we start with one distinction: must all view access go through the relational engine

Right now my opinion is that we should layer all our development over relational engine indeed. The value is that what we develop doesn't care from where it come, thats relational engine responsability. Other advantage is interoperability, if everything is layer on it we have a common backbone making interoperability of the system we develop much easier.

> and must all underlying data be stored in it

This is the part where i am more on the fence, relational engine performance as the central block is paramount to the success of the software we build and as such i even wonder if there is one good answer for that. That the materialization aspect and taking a stance there not backed by evidence seems pointless.

For me the way to not having to answer the second part is abstraction + API. No object goes out of the API everything layer on top CRUD through the api and never manage any object itself. That way whats how we structure underneath doesn't matter. However abstraction has a performance cost aswell and come with other tradeoff.

Maybe we could research other projects with similitude to see what realisticly achievable on the performance side and how they achieved it ?

### Assistant

Yes. I researched four useful comparisons. **They support a common data API with several storage strategies, but they do not establish the performance of our TypeScript implementation.**

| Project | What is relevant to us | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SQLite virtual tables** | The same query API can access ordinary tables, external files, in-memory structures or computed data. Providers receive query constraints so they can avoid retrieving everything. | Providers still differ in supported writes and indexing. A uniform API must expose those capabilities honestly. [Documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/vtab.html) |
| **Datomic** | Its entity API provides lazy, immutable views of a particular database revision. Storage and caching remain behind that API. | A consistent snapshot can be older than the latest state; cached access and cold access have different costs. [Entities](https://docs.datomic.com/reference/entities.html), [caching](https://docs.datomic.com/operation/caching.html) |
| **Flecs** | An entity/component system that groups entities with the same components and caches matching groups for repeated queries. Particularly relevant to our model. | Caching consumes memory and adds maintenance work. Its documentation also shows how hierarchy layout can substantially change performance. [Queries](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Queries.html), [hierarchies](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/HierarchiesManual.html) |
| **DuckDB** | Queries can run directly over existing data without first importing a second database copy. Execution processes batches of values. | These optimizations target analytical workloads; they do not establish interactive graph-editing performance. [Direct querying](https://duckdb.org/2021/05/14/sql-on-pandas), [execution](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/internals/vector) |

There is measurable evidence that abstraction can pay for itself. In DuckDB’s published 2021 experiment using a roughly 1 GB TPC-H dataset in Google Colab, one grouped aggregation took **0.43 seconds with single-threaded DuckDB versus 0.84 seconds with Pandas**, both operating on Pandas data. The authors attribute this to grouping and aggregation in one pass. This is a historical workload-specific result; we have not reproduced it locally. [Benchmark and methodology](https://duckdb.org/2021/05/14/sql-on-pandas)

For our design, I would distinguish **keeping authoritative objects private** from **requiring a separate API call for every value**. Handles, revision-bound read views or read-only batches could preserve ownership without creating another mutable domain model in each consumer. That is a proposal to test against your stricter handle-only approach. Call granularity especially matters across process boundaries: SQLite explicitly distinguishes cheap in-process calls from repeated client/server round trips. [SQLite’s explanation](https://www.sqlite.org/np1queryprob.html)

My inference is that we can keep storage flexible, but must define identity, mutation ownership, consistency, freshness and source capabilities early. The API cannot make those semantics disappear.

One consequence for predicates: an arbitrary TypeScript function is not automatically a query the engine can optimize or send to an external source. We must decide how much of it the engine can understand, and what happens when evaluation requires fetching data. SQLite and DuckDB explicitly expose constraints or query expressions to enable that optimization. [SQLite planning](https://www.sqlite.org/vtab.html), [DuckDB planning](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/internals/overview)

**My recommended next step is a small measured comparison**, using Activity board filtering, graph traversal and an edit reflected in several views. Compare handles and batch reads, with direct provider access versus an engine-owned materialization behind the same contract. Measure cold/warm latency, slow requests, memory, transferred bytes and update propagation; verify identical results and rejected stale writes. That would give us evidence for storage choices and concrete architecture checks without committing to one universal materialization policy.

This exchange is appended verbatim to the discussion task.

### User

### Assistant

I did miss the central issue. I reduced it to “can a database abstraction be fast?” and presented performance techniques without establishing whether those projects solve your architectural problem. The experiment proposal followed from that incomplete framing.

My understanding of your proposal is:

- **The relational engine is the common foundation for development.** Systems consume its model and operations; they do not need source-specific access or their own competing representation of the same data.
- **That does not require a second graph-shaped copy of everything.** Existing data must be accessible through the common model, while its physical representation and ownership remain hidden behind the API.
- **The API protects that freedom.** Consumers should not retain implementation objects, mutate them independently, or become responsible for synchronizing them with the engine.

The question I should investigate is: **how can one shared entity/component/relation model provide access to heterogeneous data without imposing duplicate storage, synchronization machinery, or excessive access costs?** That includes identity, reads, mutations and change propagation together.

My research did not establish that combination. DuckDB aggregation timings, for example, tell us very little about whether this foundation works for an extensible application. I also incorrectly translated your “no object goes out” into a “handle-only” design that you had not specified.

I am dropping the experimentation proposal. Before choosing examples, I need to identify systems that actually use a common application data model over different underlying representations, then examine how they preserve that boundary and what restrictions make it practical. Storage strategy comes after that understanding.

### User

> can a database abstraction be fast

Relational engine is not a database that the main issue.

### Assistant

Yes. I was treating the relational engine as a database and reasoning outward from storage. That category error shaped both my research and my proposed next steps.

You are discussing **the foundation through which application systems expose, access and operate on data and relationships**, independent of where that data comes from. Persistence is one possible concern underneath it. Materialization also concerns how existing or computed application state becomes accessible through that foundation; it is not automatically database replication.

That changes the research target to **application runtimes and shared object/component models**: how they mediate access to live state, preserve identity, route operations and propagate changes without requiring parallel representations everywhere.

I need to ground that understanding in our engine's actual responsibilities and contracts before making another recommendation. My previous database comparisons did not do that.

### User

> I need to ground that understanding in our engine's actual responsibilities and contracts before making another recommendation. My previous database comparisons did not do that.

I would not do that because it would only muddy your context considering the current state of relational engine.

I think the first step is picking project with similitude to relational engine fundamentals.

### User

projects

### Assistant

I would shortlist **Blender RNA, Eclipse EMF, OpenUSD and Flecs**, each for a specific similarity:

| Project | Similar fundamentals | Important difference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **[Blender — RNA](https://developer.blender.org/docs/features/core/rna/)** | A common runtime description of data, properties and functions serves the UI, scripting and other application systems. Accessors can expose underlying structures or computed values, with update notifications. | It is built around Blender's application model; we must examine where its abstraction applies and where internal systems bypass it. |
| **[Eclipse Modeling Framework — EMF](https://eclipse.dev/emf/)** | A shared model of types, attributes and references supports reflective access, change notifications and reusable editors. Different tools operate on the same model. | It exposes model objects. Its command-based editing discipline is particularly worth examining because direct modifications remain possible. [Editing model](https://help.eclipse.org/latest/topic/org.eclipse.emf.doc/references/overview/EMF.Edit.html) |
| **[OpenUSD](https://openusd.org/release/intro.html)** | Multiple inputs are composed into a common scene model with typed properties and relationships. Consumers access the composed result, with selective loading to control the working set. | Its primary purpose is scene description and interchange. We should study its composition and access model without assuming its domain semantics fit ours. |
| **[Flecs](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/EntitiesComponents.html)** | Entities, components and relationships form a common foundation for systems and queries. Relationships are part of that model rather than an additional representation. [Relationships](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Relationships.html) | It permits direct component references, including mutable ones, so it does not establish the encapsulation you are considering. |

**I would start with Blender RNA and EMF** for the shared application foundation. OpenUSD is the complementary candidate for composition and materialization; Flecs for entity/component/relationship semantics.

At this stage, these are candidates for examination. We have not established that any one satisfies the complete set of fundamentals we want.

### User

flecs is the best pick. The challenge we have though is materialization that i don't think they have at a glance but i'd like you to confirm it.

### Assistant

**Your impression is broadly correct: I found no built-in external-data materialization layer equivalent to what we need.** Flecs’ documented query model operates on entities and components already present in its ECS world. It does not describe a provider contract that discovers external data, loads it on demand and keeps it synchronized. That conclusion is based on its documented architecture and APIs. [Query model](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Queries.html)

There are useful nuances:

- **Storage choices and sharing:** Flecs supports dense and sparse component storage, and inheritance can share a component value between entities. These address storage within the ECS world. [Component traits](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/ComponentTraits.html)
- **Existing representations and computed fields:** its *opaque type* support lets custom callbacks describe and read/write types whose layout Flecs does not understand. Its example operates on a standalone native object and exposes a computed `result` field without storing that field. So Flecs does offer a relevant mechanism for exposing data without duplicating its representation. [Opaque type API](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/group__c__addons__meta.html), [example](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/examples-reflection-ser_opaque_type.html)
- **Query caching:** Flecs can retain matching storage groups to accelerate queries. This does not supply fetching or synchronization with external sources. [Caching](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Queries.html#performance-and-caching)

The boundary matters: **describing and accessing an existing value does not automatically make an external collection of values queryable as entities and relationships.** The opaque example establishes the former; it does not establish the latter.

For us, the unresolved responsibility remains deciding which external things become visible in the relational model, whether their values are accessed directly or materialized, and how changes and writes reach their owner.

I would keep Flecs as our main reference for entities, components, relationships and queries, with **opaque reflection as the next mechanism to examine closely**. It offers a concrete starting point for the representation question, while leaving the wider materialization policy open.

### User

> I would keep Flecs as our main reference for entities, components, relationships and queries, with **opaque reflection as the next mechanism to examine closely**. It offers a concrete starting point for the representation question, while leaving the wider materialization policy open.  



I would aswell its a really good match considering it has relationship.



Can we find projects around materialization then to have the other part of the "equation" ?

### Assistant

Yes. **Hydra 2.0 looks like the strongest complement to Flecs**, with Apache Sling and EMF Views covering other useful parts.

| Project | Relevant mechanism | Limit of the comparison |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **OpenUSD — Hydra 2.0** | A common API exposes scene structure and values on demand. Layers can transform or combine data lazily, and change notifications identify precisely what became invalid. Separate caching layers can retain selected results. [Architecture](https://openusd.org/release/api/_page__hydra__getting__started__guide.html), [caching](https://openusd.org/release/api/class_hdsi_locator_caching_scene_index.html) | Its scene-index API primarily supplies data to consumers such as renderers. It does not by itself give us a general CRUD contract for editing the original sources. |
| **Apache Sling — Resource Providers** | Different sources contribute to one virtual resource tree. Consumers use a common resolver; providers implement access and, where supported, creation, updates, deletion and refresh. This is a useful reference for keeping operations routed through the abstraction to the owning source. [Resources](https://sling.apache.org/documentation/the-sling-engine/resources.html), [resolver contract](https://sling.apache.org/apidocs/sling14/org/apache/sling/api/resource/ResourceResolver.html) | Its organizing model is hierarchical. Commits spanning several providers are not atomic, and external changes need not appear immediately. |
| **EMF Views** | Combines existing models through virtual elements that refer to the originals, and can add associations between them. Consumers navigate and query the resulting view as an ordinary model. This directly addresses presenting a unified relational model without making an independent copy of every source element. [User guide](https://www.atlanmod.org/emfviews/manual/user.html) | Sources must already be exposed as EMF models. We would still need to establish how arbitrary external sources and edits fit that boundary. |

**Hydra is particularly relevant to your hesitation about one universal materialization policy.** Its documentation describes several reasons to retain data—repeated access, shared dependencies and expensive transformations—and deliberately makes caching selective. It also makes cache correctness depend on explicit invalidation of affected data. [Caching rationale](https://openusd.org/release/api/class_hdsi_locator_caching_scene_index.html)

I would therefore examine **Flecs + Hydra first**: Flecs for the common entity/component/relationship model, Hydra for supplying that model through deferred access, transformations and selective retention. **Sling would be the complementary reference for CRUD and source ownership.**

### User

nothing really catch my eye.

### Assistant

A more concrete candidate is **Linux’s Virtual File System (VFS), including FUSE**.

The similarity I see is that applications operate through one common API while different implementations own the underlying data and behavior. VFS routes operations to those implementations and manages the representations needed to access them. [VFS architecture](https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/vfs.html)

Three mechanisms are particularly relevant:

- **The complete logical space need not be materialized.** The directory-entry cache normally contains only part of the accessible namespace. Missing entries are resolved through the responsible filesystem when needed.
- **Identity, metadata and contents are separate concerns.** Representing an accessible file does not require loading its contents. Open handles keep the necessary access state alive. [Lookup and file objects](https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/vfs.html)
- **A common API can support different retention policies.** FUSE supports direct access that bypasses the page cache, cached reads, immediate forwarding of writes, and deferred writeback. Those choices have explicit consistency constraints; deferred writeback assumes changes pass through FUSE. [FUSE I/O modes](https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/fuse/fuse-io.html)

That is closer to the part of our problem I want a reference for: **something can belong to the common logical model without requiring all of its data to be copied into a second managed representation.** There is still access metadata and potentially cached data; their scope and lifetime are separate choices.

The limitation is clear: filesystem operations do not give us Flecs-style component queries or arbitrary relationships. We would study VFS for **access, ownership and materialization boundaries**, alongside Flecs for the relational model. I would examine that separation before expanding the shortlist again.

### User

yep with the rational you gave it match but only because of the rational and with the reserve that its a domain specific solution when we need a generic approch without any domain dependency.

### Assistant

Yes. **VFS gives us a reference for particular mechanisms; it does not establish that those mechanisms form a generic solution.**

The distinction should be explicit:

- **Potentially reusable:** resolving data on demand, retaining selected representations, tracking their validity, and routing mutations to their owner.
- **Domain-specific:** file paths, directories, byte streams, filesystem metadata and filesystem-specific consistency rules.

Even a pluggable provider API can carry domain dependencies. If its identity, traversal or mutation rules assume a filesystem tree, adding more providers does not make it generic.

For our engine, I would propose a concrete acceptance criterion: **a filesystem, a task system and a running application’s state can each contribute through the same contracts, without the core knowing which domain it is handling.** Their domain rules remain with their contributors. The core owns the common semantics and enforces the contracts; it does not become an unstructured forwarding layer.

That also gives us a stricter research criterion: look for abstractions actually used across unrelated domains, and inspect where domain knowledge enters them.

So I would retain VFS as a bounded reference alongside Flecs. **The generic materialization part remains unresolved**, including whether its common semantics can support the different sources without forcing duplication or leaking their domain rules.

### User

you want to give a shot to a last search with the additional criterion ?

### Assistant

**Eclipse Epsilon’s Model Connectivity layer (EMC) is the strongest candidate from this last pass.** It provides a common API for selecting elements by type, reading/writing properties, creating/deleting elements and identifying their owner. [EMC architecture](https://eclipse.dev/epsilon/doc/emc/)

Three things make it relevant:

- **No mandatory second object representation.** Drivers can operate on native objects. The authors explicitly rejected compulsory wrappers after observing memory and performance costs. That is useful design evidence, although they provide no figures we can transfer to our engine. [Design rationale](https://eclipse.dev/epsilon/doc/emc/#assumptions-about-the-underlying-modelling-technologies)
- **Materialization can vary behind the boundary.** Its CDO driver supports fetching elements on access, configurable batches and prefetching informed by previous traversal. This demonstrates selective loading behind the shared API. [CDO driver](https://eclipse.dev/epsilon/doc/articles/cdo-emc/)
- **The contract accommodates different application domains.** Epsilon reports uses in railway analysis, business-process modelling and library metadata. These go beyond supporting different file formats, although its ecosystem remains centred on model engineering. [Documented uses](https://eclipse.dev/epsilon/users/open-source/)

**The important mismatch is that EMC allows native objects through its API.** It does not enforce your proposed boundary where consumers only manipulate data through API operations. Loading remains driver-specific, too; the documentation does not establish a complete cross-source consistency policy. [EMC contracts](https://eclipse.dev/epsilon/doc/emc/)

I would keep **Flecs for entities, components and relationships, and EMC for independence from underlying representations**. That is the most relevant pair I found. The next useful examination is how EMC avoids duplication, and how much of that approach remains usable when objects must stay behind our API.

### User

i am reading the doc of eclipse you linked and its not clicking for me honestly. Value of their abstraction seems really limited and explanation just doesn't connect to what we are doing even with your rational.

I read the API at the start and it feels inefficient and hacky.

### Assistant

**I overstated EMC’s relevance.** Its main value is letting Epsilon programs use the same operations across different modelling technologies. The generic objects, string type names and property getters/setters serve that purpose. [EMC documentation](https://eclipse.dev/epsilon/doc/emc/)

For our problem, the API shown leaves three substantial gaps:

- **Efficient batch access:** `getAllOfType` followed by property reads does not express a complete request that a provider could optimize. A driver might optimize internally, but that contract doesn’t establish how.
- **Representation independence:** passing native objects avoids wrapping them, but leaves consumers holding source-specific representations. That doesn’t establish the boundary you proposed.
- **Materialization management:** `load`, `store` and ownership don’t explain what should be fetched, retained, indexed or invalidated when underlying data changes.

The diagram alone cannot establish actual runtime performance. But it gives us too little evidence for the problem we’re trying to solve, and I stretched the connection.

**The missing reference would explain how externally owned data participates in entity/component/relationship queries, with useful control over what must exist locally.** For example, can the engine know a relationship exists and query it without first copying every component value? What happens when the external owner changes that data?

Those are the mechanisms we need to understand. I would put EMC aside and keep Flecs as the solid reference we have, with the external-data/materialization part explicitly unresolved.

### User

ok, another point i want to discuss is concept minimization. Without going to the extrem i want as much as possible keep the number of concept used by relational engine in its "data model" at the right balance.

Right now i have some doubt around that specific aspect. Among things i have doubt on Component vs data type. Object vs entity.

### Assistant

**I would try to keep one notion of identity and one system for describing values.** A separate concept should justify itself through different behavior: what can be referenced, attached, queried, changed or removed.

For **object vs entity**, I see two meanings of “object”:

- Something with an identity that remains the same when its contents change: I would call that an **entity**, without introducing another category.
- A structured value, such as a record containing coordinates: its structure belongs to its **data type**. It does not automatically need an independent identity.

A nested value can still be edited through its owner. Being editable does not, by itself, make it an entity. Likewise, an entity’s identity does not require us to allocate or copy all its data locally; materialization remains a separate question.

For **component vs data type**, we should compare a *component definition* with a *data type*, and a *component’s value* with other values. Otherwise, we mix definitions and instances.

The useful distinction I see is:

- A **data type** describes what a value means and which values are valid.
- A **component** expresses something an entity carries, whose presence can participate in composition and queries.

Those roles do not necessarily require two separate kinds of type declaration.

For example, if creation time and modification time are separately attached facts, both can use `Timestamp`. They share a value type but need distinguishable attachment roles. Conversely, `Timestamp` should also work inside a larger record without acquiring component behavior.

**My starting proposal would therefore be:**

- Drop **Object** as a separate engine concept if it only duplicates entity or structured value.
- Use the same **data type system** for component values, nested fields and other values.
- Keep **component attachment** as meaningful behavior, while questioning whether a separate **component-type definition** adds anything beyond a named role and its value type.

The next thing I would examine is exactly that last point: what information would be lost if component definitions reused ordinary type definitions? That gives us a concrete way to minimize concepts without hiding necessary distinctions.

### User

I think i need to understand typescript / javascript a bit better honestly to decide how we organize the concepts of relational engine. Not that i want relational engine to follow the data model of those language but I think it would make for an usefull feature if it overlapped just enough so we don't need to have our own object model internally.

First thing i wonder is if a typescript object == a javascript object ? Does every typescript objects have a prototype reference ?

### Assistant

**Yes: at runtime, an object created by TypeScript code is a JavaScript object.** TypeScript adds checking before execution; it does not introduce a separate runtime object model. Type annotations, interfaces and type aliases are erased. [TypeScript documentation](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/basic-types.html#erased-types)

For example:

```ts
type Position = { x: number; y: number };

const position: Position = { x: 10, y: 20 };

Object.getPrototypeOf(position) === Object.prototype; // true
```

Here, `Position` tells TypeScript what to check. It does **not** create a `Position` object at runtime, attach a type descriptor to `position`, or give it a special prototype.

**An object does not necessarily have a prototype pointing to another object.** Every ordinary JavaScript object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link whose value is either:

- Another object.
- `null`, meaning there is no prototype.

When a property is missing from the object itself, JavaScript normally looks for it along that prototype chain. This is how inherited properties and methods work. [JavaScript specification](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/ordinary-and-exotic-objects-behaviours.html#sec-ordinary-object-internal-methods-and-internal-slots)

Some examples:

| Object | Its prototype |
|---|---|
| An ordinary object literal, such as `{ x: 10 }` | `Object.prototype` |
| An object created with `Object.create(null)` | `null` |
| `Object.prototype` itself | `null` |

You inspect that link with `Object.getPrototypeOf(value)`. It is separate from a regular property named `prototype`; objects do not all have such a property. [Object operations](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/fundamental-objects.html#sec-object.getprototypeof)

For relational engine, this means **we can use ordinary JavaScript objects internally without inventing another object representation**. However, their TypeScript types will not automatically be available for runtime inspection or validation. A prototype provides inheritance; by itself, it does not describe required fields or their allowed types.

### Assistant

Yes—**the graph should model relational engine’s own concepts**.

We would start with **Entity, Object, Component and Data type** as candidates, then describe their relationships and decide which distinctions are useful. Drawing four nodes would not commit us to keeping four concepts.

The dependency graph is a possible canvas. The capability to check is whether it supports named relationships: “has a type,” “attached to” and “contains” mean different things from “depends on.” Its dependency semantics should not dictate the conceptual model we design.

### User

First thing are we able to reuse the dependency graph view by itself without bringing everything with it ? is it correctly encapsulated ?

### Assistant

**Yes, we can reuse the core graph without bringing the application with it. The complete view is only partly encapsulated.**

The core is `DependencyGraphElement`, with its own public export. It accepts nodes, edges and a selection callback, plus optional layout and viewport settings. Its imports are Lit—the web-component library—and small shared styling, theme and utility modules. It does not import the repository UI, planning system or relational engine service. [Component API](C:/Users/vince/Documents/GitHub/Btr/TheBroccoli/Systems/Depth2/RelationalUi/Depth2/DependencyGraph/index.ts:20)

There are three qualifications:

- **The surrounding controls are outside the component.** The zoom toolbar, orientation switch, Focus/Connected tabs, drag-to-pan and viewport-state persistence are assembled in a HarnessApp wrapper. Reusing the full experience requires separating that reusable composition from the application. [View wrapper](C:/Users/vince/Documents/GitHub/Btr/TheBroccoli/Systems/Depth4/HarnessApp/Depth1/Browser/repository-graph.ts:16)
- **Some host assumptions remain.** It expects shared theme values and uses styles in the surrounding DOM. Its default node tooltip also assumes a connected Node editor, although no Node editor is technically required. That wording is an unnecessary semantic dependency. [Rendering](C:/Users/vince/Documents/GitHub/Btr/TheBroccoli/Systems/Depth2/RelationalUi/Depth2/DependencyGraph/index.ts:72)
- **The package is broader than the component.** It belongs to RelationalUi, whose package declares engine, language-support and other dependencies. Importing the graph entry does not load all those modules, but installing the package still brings that dependency footprint. [Package](C:/Users/vince/Documents/GitHub/Btr/TheBroccoli/Systems/Depth2/RelationalUi/package.json:236)

For our concept graph, there is also a separate functional limitation: **edges currently have no labels or relationship kinds**, and the layout interprets them as dependencies. [Edge contract](C:/Users/vince/Documents/GitHub/Btr/TheBroccoli/Systems/Depth2/RelationalUi/Depth2/DependencyGraph/model.ts:17)

### Assistant

Yes. **We can divide the design into a few questions we answer separately, then examine how the answers fit together.** Your document mixes capabilities, guarantees, and qualities that should apply everywhere. That helps explain why trying to turn the whole list into concepts feels difficult.

I’d organize the discussion into four areas:

| Area | Question to resolve | Needs it brings together |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning and structure** | What can we express about things and their relationships? | Types, relations, logical structure, composition, and your latest point about composition determining type. |
| **Access and knowledge** | What can we know or use without owning or fully loading it? | Source independence, partial information, materialization, lazy access. |
| **Change and guarantees** | What changes can we request, and what can the engine promise? | CRUD where possible, invariants, preparing changes, cancellation, atomicity. |
| **Cooperation** | How do independently developed or controlled parts work together? | External contributions, events, cooperating engines, decentralized authority. |

**Performance, observability, domain independence, and keeping concepts few and meaningful apply to all four.** They become questions we revisit with each proposed answer.

These areas overlap. For example, “all or nothing” changes and “data we don’t control” meet at a boundary we must explicitly resolve. Dividing the discussion helps us identify that boundary.

For each area, I suggest we:
1. Describe one concrete situation and the outcome we want.
2. Identify what the engine must guarantee, what depends on external participants, and what remains unknown.
3. Introduce only the concepts needed to explain that behavior.
4. Check whether those concepts still make sense in the other areas.

**I would start with access and knowledge.** It directly addresses your central intention: systems should work through the engine without needing to know where their information comes from.

Our first situation could be:

> Something is managed outside the engine. I want to refer to it, connect it to something else, and read one piece of information without loading everything.

We can work through what must be possible in that situation and who is responsible for each part. That gives us a small, concrete piece of the engine to define while leaving storage and implementation choices open.
